# How it works

For every learner, all the time, the CRM works out four things: how likely they are to buy if the team does nothing,
which step would change that and pay for itself, whether that step deserves one of the day's few call slots or a
share of the month's discount money, and what all of it is worth in rupees. It keeps learning from its own results
without counting its own follow-ups as lead quality. This page explains each part in plain words, with the formula
where one helps, and names the experiment that tests it ([RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md) has the numbers and the
comparisons with other methods). The people who use the CRM need none of this: its **Start here** page explains what
it does and where each of them begins, in plain words.

## 1. The lead score

**What it means.** The score is the chance that the person buys within 14 days *if the team does nothing now*,
shown as 0 to 100. "If we do nothing" matters: the CRM's own emails, coupons and calls must never be counted as
lead quality (see the learning loop below), and it is what lets the CRM say what comes in anyway (section 4).

**How it is made.** Two parts (`backend/app/ml/lead_model.py`):

```
logit P(buy within 14 days | lead, no step now)
    = a * logit(base(x))                  base model, trained once
    + b + sum_j w_j * s_j(x)              live layer, learned from this CRM's own outcomes
    + effect of time away + effect of lead age
```

- The **base model** is trained at the first start on 60,000 simulated leads that carry every signal the website
  records: profile, visits, time on site, video, pricing page, brochure, chat, webinar, wishlist, cart, checkout,
  enquiry, email clicks, WhatsApp and contact consent. Logistic regression and gradient boosting are compared on a
  held-out 20%; logistic regression is kept unless boosting is clearly better (lower log-loss).
- The **live layer** re-calibrates the base model to this business: how strongly the base score carries over (`a`),
  the overall level of buying (`b`) and small corrections for the strongest signals (`w`), shrunk towards zero so
  they only move as far as real outcomes support. How much time away and the lead's age lower the chance is learned
  too, not set by hand.

**When it changes.** Every tracked event re-scores the learner at once (a click on the pricing page shows on the
CRM within a second), and every lead is re-scored on a timer because time away lowers the chance.

**Tiers** (from `crm_settings.json`): 80 and above *Target Immediately*, 60 to 79 *Nurture via Email/WhatsApp*,
40 to 59 *Marketing Campaign*, below 40 *Low Priority*. The lead page lists the factors behind a score: what each
signal added or took away.

**No leakage.** The model uses only what the website records before anyone contacts the lead. The public X Education
dataset also has columns sales fills in after contact (Tags, Lead Quality and others) that push AUC to 0.98; they are
never used, and a test fails if one is. Tested on real data in **E1** and against published solutions in **E1b**.

## 2. Next-best-action

A score says who is likely to buy. It does not say what to do: a hot lead given a 20% coupon would often have bought
anyway, so the discount is money given away. Next-best-action (`backend/app/ml/nba_core.py`, `nba.py`) estimates,
for every step the team could take, the chance to buy after that step, and picks the step that adds the most profit:

```
expected profit of step a  =  P(buy | person, a) * course fee * (1 - discount of a) - cost of a
extra profit of step a     =  expected profit of a - expected profit of doing nothing
chosen step                =  the allowed step with the largest extra profit after the prices of a call slot and
                              of discount money (section 3), or nothing when none is positive
```

The steps are: do nothing, an information email, an email with a 10% or 20% coupon, a counsellor call, a WhatsApp
message (costs and discounts in `crm_settings.json`).

- **The model** is a logistic S-learner with step-by-context interactions: `logit P(buy | x, a) = beta * c(x) +
  gamma_a * c(x)`, where `c(x)` is a small context built on the lead score (the score itself, price-sensitive
  occupations, high intent, cart or enquiry, professionals, email engagement, WhatsApp opt-in, low engagement).
  Each `gamma_a` reads as "how much step a moves the odds for people like this", so every decision can be explained.
  A flexible gradient-boosting model competes with it in the learning loop; the better one on held-out decisions
  is used.
- **Consent first.** A step the person has not allowed is never chosen: no email after "do not email", no call
  without a phone number or after "do not call", no WhatsApp without opt-in, nothing at all for a lead closed as
  lost or for the 5% control group.
- **What the team sees.** Every step is chosen on its expected value (chance of buying x fee, after the discount and
  the step's cost, and the call-slot price), but lead-level screens show only chances of buying and how much a step
  changes them: nobody has paid anything yet, so a per-lead "profit" would mislead. Rupee totals appear only as the
  owner's forecasts (Pipeline totals, Overview, Planner) and on the Next-best-action page.
- **One open coupon per person, and at most one a week.** While someone still holds a coupon they can use (from the
  CRM or the team), no second coupon is chosen or given: discounts would only stack on the same purchase. After a
  coupon, the next one waits 7 days whether it was used or not (`coupon_gap_days` in `crm_settings.json`), so
  coupons do not teach people to wait for the next one. Every coupon has its own code (a
  readable name for the discount and five random characters, for example SMARTSTART20-K7Q2M) that works only for that
  person, once.
- **No step twice in a row by hand.** The team cannot send a person the same email step again within 24 hours
  (`manual_repeat` in `crm_settings.json`), or plan a second call or WhatsApp message while the first one is still
  waiting in Today's actions; the lead page says when the step can be taken again.
- **Learning by design.** 15% of automatic decisions are random among the allowed steps, and every decision is
  logged with the probability it had. That makes honest evaluation and retraining possible (inverse-propensity
  weighting) without a separate experiment. The setting is `exploration_rate`; what the random steps cost is
  measured in **E8b**.
- **The decision receipt.** Each decision is stored with every option, its chance to buy, its extra profit and the
  prices it was charged, so the lead page shows exactly why the CRM did what it did.

Tested on a real randomised email experiment in **E2** and, with the assumptions about the world deliberately
broken, in **E2b**.

## 3. Two scarce resources, priced: call slots and discount money

A business has two things it cannot hand out to everyone: counsellor time and discount money. Next-best-action
decides one learner at a time, as triggers arrive, so a plain limit hands both out first come, first served: a call
or a coupon that adds a little in the morning takes what an evening lead needed far more. The CRM gives each a
price, worked out again at every decision, and a step is chosen only when it beats its price (the bid price of
airline revenue management, Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004).

### Call slots

The team can make only so many calls a day (`daily_call_capacity`, 8 for one counsellor). What a call adds is not
its whole value, only what it adds over the best step without a call, because an email is often nearly as good
(`backend/app/ml/capacity.py`):

```
call advantage   d = extra profit of a call - max(extra profit of every other allowed step, including nothing)
slot price       the smallest x for which the calls with d > x, expected in the rest of today, fit into the
                 slots that are left
```

The expected arrivals come from the CRM's own decision log: every automatic decision of the last 7 days where a call
was possible stores its `d` and its time of day. With `R` the share of a day's call-worthy decisions that usually
arrive after now, `D` the number of days seen and `S` the slots left:

```
k     = floor(S * D / R)
price = the (k + 1)-th largest d of the window   (0 when there are fewer)
```

So the price falls when slots are left late in the day and rises when they are being used up early; it is infinite
when no slot is left and zero when demand is below capacity. Until 50 decisions with a possible call exist, or with
`call_capacity.policy` set to `fcfs`, the price is 0. The hard daily cap stays as a backstop.

**Result (E7).** On simulated days with known true effects, when call-worthy decisions outnumber the slots 2 to 8
times, first come, first served captures 41% to 70% of the value of the call slots that the best allocation with
hindsight gets; the re-solved slot price captures 95% to 97%. With spare capacity it changes nothing.

### Discount money

Without a budget, a coupon goes out whenever it adds more profit than its discount costs. The owner can set a
monthly discount budget on the Planner page (`backend/app/ml/budget.py`). A coupon costs money only when it is used:

```
expected discount  c = P(buy | coupon) * course fee * discount
coupon advantage   v = extra profit of the best allowed coupon
                       - max(extra profit of every other allowed step, including nothing; a call net of its price)
money left         B = budget - discounts given this month - expected discount of the coupons still open
price              the (k + 1)-th largest v / c of the last 7 days' decisions, with k the most coupons (largest
                   v / c first) whose c fits B * D / T     (D days in the window, T days left in the month)
```

Every step is then counted net of its prices: `extra profit - slot price * [call] - discount price * expected
discount`. The price rises when money is going fast and falls when it is left over; it is 0 with no budget or when
there is money for every coupon that pays, and when the money is gone, coupons stop until next month. Until 30
decisions where a coupon paid have been seen, the price is 0 and coupons simply stop when the money is used up.

**Result (E9).** With a budget of 10% to 50% of what every paying coupon would cost, spending it first come, first
served gets 37% to 62% of the value of the best single price chosen with hindsight; the re-solved price gets 97% to
100%, a fixed price set at the start of the month 89% to 95%, and the usual cart-recovery rule (a 10% coupon for every
left cart) loses money. The re-solved price stays within the budget (95% to 97% of it used, in truth).

**What the team sees.** The decision receipt shows a step net of its prices ("+₹8,251 before the call slot price of
₹324"); Today's actions and the Next-best-action page show the call meter (calls used, slots left, the price now);
the Planner page shows the discount budget (given, promised in open coupons, left, the price now).

## 4. The pipeline in rupees

**The problem.** A usual pipeline shows stages, and a forecast that multiplies each deal by a probability. That
probability is learned from leads the team worked, so it already includes the team's work: the forecast cannot say
what comes in anyway and what the team's work adds. And a list sorted by score puts first the people who would buy
anyway, where the team adds least.

**What the CRM shows** (`backend/app/services/money.py`, the Pipeline page). For every open lead, from the same
numbers as next-best-action:

```
comes in anyway    = P(buy within 14 days | no step) * course fee     (the lead score, in rupees)
the team can add   = extra profit of the best step now, net of the prices of section 3
```

- At the top: what comes in anyway from all open leads, what the team can still add and with how many leads.
- Each stage shows both numbers, and its cards are ordered by what the team can add (or by score, if preferred).
- Each card has one line, for example "+₹6,320 with a 20% coupon email", and **Do it** takes that step at once
  (logged like any other decision, with its receipt).
- **No discount needed** marks leads who are more likely than not to buy anyway and for whom no coupon would add
  profit: a coupon there only gives money away.
- Leads in the control group, customers and lost leads have nothing to add.

**Result (E9).** On simulated pipelines of 1,200 open leads with known truth, "comes in anyway" is within 0.1% of the
true total and "the team can add" within 2%. When the team has time for 5% to 40% of the leads, working them in this
order adds 89% to 93% of the most it could add, against 4% to 62% for highest score first and 24% to 50% at random.
Of the leads marked "No discount needed", 91% truly lose money with a coupon.

## 5. The coupon guard

**The problem.** Discounts given by hand to "close" warm leads mostly go to people who would have paid in full.

**What the CRM does** (`money.coupon_check`, the Coupons page). Before a personal coupon is given, the dialog shows
what it would do for that person, from the same numbers as next-best-action:

```
chance without    p0 = the lead score
chance with       p1 = P(buy | coupon), from next-best-action's model (its 10% or 20% coupon, the nearer one)
expected discount    = p1 * course fee * discount
extra profit         = p1 * course fee * (1 - discount) - p0 * course fee
```

- If the coupon pays for itself, it is given as usual.
- If it does not, the dialog says why ("97% chance to buy without a coupon: about ₹2,729 of discount, 99% of it to
  someone who would have paid in full") and the coupon is given only if someone confirms with **Give it anyway**.
- If it would go over what is left of the month's discount budget, the dialog says so, with the same confirmation.
- A coupon for a lead in the control group is never given: it would spoil the CRM's own measurement.
- A second coupon for someone who still holds an open one is never given either: withdraw the first one to change it.

Every coupon given by hand is stored with its expected discount, so it counts against the budget like the CRM's own.

**Result (E9).** Of coupons a counsellor would give to the warmest 10% of leads, the guard stops all of them, and
98% to 100% truly lose money; of coupons for every left cart it stops 59% to 67%, 95% to 96% of them rightly, which
turns those coupons from a loss into a profit; of coupons for leads picked at random it stops 36% to 45%, 74% to 80%
of them rightly.

## 6. The owner's planner

**The problem.** The owner's questions (what does the team's work bring in, should we hire another counsellor, how
much discount money is worth setting aside) are usually answered from reports that cannot separate what would have
come in anyway.

**What the CRM shows** (`backend/app/services/planner.py`, the Planner page), from its own decision log and its
control group:

- **The month in rupees:** revenue so far, what comes in anyway from the open leads, what the team can add, and the
  discount the CRM's decisions kept this week against a coupon for every left cart.
- **What the team's work adds:** the share who bought within 30 days among leads the CRM worked on against the
  control group it never contacts. The control group is chosen at random, so the difference is what the team's steps
  add; it is shown with its 95% interval and in rupees at the average fee paid.
- **Should we hire another counsellor?** Last week's decisions are replayed with 8 more call slots a day (one more
  counsellor): the extra calls the CRM's own rule would then have made, each worth what it adds over the best step
  without a call, against what a counsellor costs a month (a setting on the page).
- **The discount budget:** set or remove the monthly budget, see what the coupons that pay would cost in a month
  without a limit, and what ₹10,000 more would add.

**Result (E9).** The estimate of what one more counsellor adds is within 11% below to 3% above the true extra profit
of the extra slots (call demand 1 to 8 times today's slots); the value of today's slots within 4%. The estimate of
what 20% more discount money adds is within 12% below to 15% above the truth when the budget is tight; when there is
already money for every coupon that pays, both are close to zero.

## 7. A learning loop that does not fool itself

**The problem.** A CRM that retrains its score on "who bought" learns its own follow-ups as if they were lead
quality: hot leads get emails, coupons and calls, those make them buy, and the retrained model concludes that people
like them are even hotter. The usual check, accuracy on recent data, then picks the inflated model, because the same
follow-ups shaped that data. And when next-best-action acts by a rule on the score's own signals (the pricing page,
the cart, an enquiry), the same leads always get the same step, so the decision log alone cannot tell the step from
the signal.

**What the loop does** (`backend/app/ml/learning.py`, `anchor.py`), whenever enough new outcomes are known:

1. **Data.** Every decision point with a known outcome: what the CRM knew about the lead then, what it did, and
   whether they bought within 14 days.
2. **What the CRM's work adds, measured.** The CRM runs an experiment on itself: the 5% control group is chosen by a hash,
   whatever the lead does, and never contacted, and next-best-action still logs the step it would have taken for
   them. So for each step (the information email, each coupon, the call, WhatsApp) the loop compares the leads it
   acted on with that step against the control-group leads it would have given the same step:

   ```
   lift of step a   = logit(share bought | acted on with a) - logit(share bought | control group, would have got a)
   standard error   bootstrap over people (a lead appears at several decision points)
   ```

   A step needs at least 20 decision points on each side; until then, and for campaign emails, its effect is learned
   from the data with the CRM's steps as inputs. Only the control group measures "never contacted": a lead the CRM
   leaves alone now is usually followed up at its next trigger, inside the 14 days. For the same reason the lift
   includes the follow-ups that come after the step: it is what the CRM's work adds, starting with that step, which
   is exactly what must be kept out of the score. (Which step works best on its own is measured by the random
   learning steps, on the Next-best-action page.)
3. **Learn.** The live layer is refitted with each lift fixed, and the score switches every step off:

   ```
   logit P(buy | lead, step now) = live layer(lead) + lift_a * [step a taken]     lift_a fixed, the rest fitted
   score                         = the same with no step
   ```

   Time away and lead age stay in the score; their size is learned. The lifts come only from the people a model is
   trained on (cross-fitting), so the check below stays honest.
4. **Check.** The new score and the one in use are compared on the control group: people nobody's follow-ups shaped,
   and new models are judged only on people they were not fitted on.
5. **Swap** only if the new score beats the one in use on the control group in at least 90% of bootstrap resamples.
6. **Record** every update, its numbers and its reason.

The next-best-action model is retrained in the same run from the decision log and replaced only if the lower end of
the 95% interval of its profit gain on held-out decisions is above zero.

**What the team sees** (the Learning loop page): how many outcomes the CRM has learned from, how accurate the score
is on never-contacted leads and when the next update is due; expected against actual buying of those leads, update
by update; what the team's work adds after each step, in points of buying chance; how time away changes the chance;
what the CRM has corrected in the starting model; every update with its result; how long the live steps take; and
the latest events. **Ask** answers "What do our emails and calls add?" from the same numbers.

**Result.** On real randomised data (**E3**), naive retraining over-predicts what customers do when nobody contacts
them by 2.35 points (22% of the true rate); this loop removes 88% of that bias, while the usual check would have
picked the inflated model in 50 of 50 repeats. In simulated histories of the whole CRM (**E8**), judged on learners
nobody contacted or trained on, the score over-states buying by 6%, against 31% for a naive retrain.

## 8. A/B tests that can be trusted, and winners adopted with a check

The A/B engine (`backend/app/ml/experiments.py`) follows Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020):

- Two or three email variants and a **control group that gets no email** (20% by default), so each result is the
  extra purchases the email caused, not just "A beat B".
- **Deterministic assignment** by a hash of test and person, stored with its probability, so the split can be
  re-checked and every assignment is a decision point for the learning loop.
- A **planned sample size** for the smallest lift worth finding (80% power), a **fixed 14-day window** (numbers before
  that are marked not final, so peeking cannot fool anyone), 95% Newcombe intervals, two-proportion tests with a
  Bonferroni correction for several variants, and a **sample-ratio check** that warns when the split is broken.
- **Adopting winners.** When a test is final and a variant clearly won, its wording becomes the standard information
  email for that audience, but 10% of the audience keeps the old email. The CRM keeps comparing them and switches
  back by itself if the new email turns out worse ("ship the winner with a holdback"). Variants that carry a
  discount are never adopted: whether to give a discount is next-best-action's decision per person.

Tested with thousands of simulated tests whose truth is known in **E4**.

## 9. What-if paths

For one lead, the CRM shows what would probably happen next: "if the team does this now, the learner will probably
do that in the next 3 days, and then the best next step is ..." (`backend/app/ml/paths.py`).

- **Step 1** uses exactly the numbers and the pick of the decision receipt, so the two can never disagree.
- **Reactions** come from how learners in the same lifecycle stage reacted to the same step in this CRM's history
  (bought, moved to cart or enquiry, came back, clicked, nothing), weighted by the probability of each logged
  decision. With too little history the page says so instead of guessing.
- **Step 2** is the best follow-up for the learner as they would then be, re-scored by the same models.

Tested out of time on the CRM's own history in **E5**.

## 10. Lead age and time away, learned

Hand-written decay rules ("minus 10 points a week") are common in CRMs. Here the effect of time away and of the
lead's age (days since sign-up, in buckets) is learned by the learning loop next to its own steps, and checked on the
control group like everything else. Compared with hand-set decay rules in **E6**.

## 11. The assistants and the messages

- **The website's help assistant** answers questions about courses, fees, duration and schedules only from the course
  catalogue and the FAQ (`backend/app/resources`), and offers a call with a counsellor when it cannot help. It never
  pretends to be a person.
- **Ask, the CRM's assistant**, answers questions about the CRM's own data (how many leads, sign-ups and customers,
  who to call today, the hottest leads, the pipeline in rupees, whether to hire another counsellor, the learning loop,
  the A/B tests, the CRM's impact, the call-slot price, revenue) with numbers read from the database; it can also
  draft an email or an A/B test. Gemini, when configured, phrases the answer; the numbers never come from the
  language model.
- **Messages** (emails, WhatsApp texts, call scripts) are written from templates, or by Gemini when configured,
  restricted to the catalogue's facts; a checker flags unprovable claims (salaries, guaranteed jobs, deadlines).

Without Gmail or Gemini every part still works: emails and sign-up codes are recorded in the log, and templates
write the messages. Any other mail server can stand in for Gmail (`SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`, `SMTP_SECURITY`). An email
the mail server does not take (no connection, a refused login, a daily limit) is kept as "not sent" with the reason,
shown on the lead's timeline, tried again every 10 minutes for a day (six tries at most, never after an opt-out), and a
campaign can send its failed emails again at once; delivery numbers count only emails that went out.

# Research results

What this CRM does better than common practice, how each claim was measured, and where it does not win. Every number
is produced by a script in this repository with fixed seeds (results in [`ml/results`](../ml/results), figures in
[`ml/results/figures`](../ml/results/figures)). The real-data studies and the simulations on a fixed calendar repeat
exactly; the studies built on simulated histories vary slightly from run to run (see section 5). Simulated learners
are always called simulated; claims about real behaviour rest only on the two real datasets.

**In five lines.**
(1) On the standard ed-tech lead dataset, with the same rows and inputs as every public solution we could re-run, our
score ranks leads better; with only what a new lead has, it reaches AUC 0.874, the best leak-free result we found.
(2) On a real randomised experiment, our retraining removes 88% of the bias a normal CRM gives itself and is the best
deployable method on one proper scoring rule in 49 of 50 repeats.
(3) Pricing the team's scarce call slots captures 95% to 97% of the best possible allocation in hindsight, against
41% to 70% for the usual first come, first served, when calls are in demand.
(4) Learned lead ageing beats hand-set decay rules on log-loss, with 95% intervals above zero.
(5) Counting the pipeline, the discount budget and the team's time in rupees of *extra* profit pays: in simulations
with known truth, a priced monthly discount budget gets 97% to 100% of the best allocation in hindsight (first come,
first served 37% to 62%; a coupon for every left cart loses money), working leads "most to add first" adds 89% to 93%
of the most the team could add (highest score first: 4% to 62%), and the coupon guard stops coupons that truly lose
money with 95% to 100% precision for warm leads and left carts.

## 1. The problem

An ed-tech CRM scores leads, decides who gets an email, a coupon or a counsellor's call, and retrains its score on who
enrolled. Four things make it look better than it is, and the usual checks are fooled in the same way:

| Failure | What happens | Common practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Leakage** | Scores built on fields sales fills in *after* contacting the lead (Tags, Lead Quality, Last Activity) look excellent offline and cannot score a new lead. | Most public solutions on the standard X Education dataset use them. |
| **Feedback** | Hot leads get the follow-ups, the follow-ups make them enrol, and a retrained score learns the CRM's own follow-ups as lead quality. The usual accuracy check, on data the CRM's actions shaped, prefers the inflated model. | Salesforce Einstein "analyzes your past converted leads"; HubSpot learns from opens, clicks and meetings. Neither help page describes separating the company's own outreach from lead quality. |
| **Staleness** | Leads who browse for weeks without enrolling are weaker buyers than their signals say, even right after a visit. | Hand-set decay on inactivity (HubSpot: "lose 25% or 50% after one month"; Salesforce Account Engagement: "decay scores above 50 to 50 if the last activity is more than 45 days ago"). It never touches an active old lead, and nobody checks its size. |
| **Scarce calls** | Counsellors can make only so many calls a day, but decisions arrive one at a time; a daily cap gives slots away first come, first served. | Uplift targeting with a budget is usually solved once over a whole customer list (for example Sapru 2025; Guduguntla et al. 2026), not for decisions that arrive through the day. |
| **Discounts to buyers anyway** | Coupons go to whoever left a cart or looks hot, and most of the money goes to people who would have paid in full; a monthly discount budget is spent first come, first served. | Cart-recovery flows attach a discount code to every abandoned-checkout email (for example Klaviyo's and Shopify's guides); a discount given by hand is not checked against the chance to buy without it. |
| **A forecast that includes the team** | The pipeline is valued with probabilities learned from leads the team worked, so it cannot say what comes in anyway and what the team's work adds; lists sorted by score put first the leads who would buy anyway. | HubSpot gives each deal stage a fixed win probability; Salesforce Pipeline Inspection groups deals by forecast category (Commit, Best Case), "controlled by the deal stage". |

## 2. What the CRM does instead

1. **Scores only on what a lead has when it arrives**, re-scored on every website event in real time (event to new
   score: 47 to 74 ms median over HTTP, 41 to 63 ms inside the server; Einstein's help page says scores are
   "updated at least every six hours").
2. **Retraining is told what the CRM did** (email, coupon, call, WhatsApp, campaign) and reads the score with it
   switched off: the chance to buy if we do nothing now. The effect of each next-best-action step is not left to the
   model: it is measured from the CRM's own experiment (leads acted on against leads of the never-contacted control
   group that it would have treated the same way) and fixed while the score is refitted.
3. **Time effects are learned, not set by hand**: time since the last visit and the lead's age.
4. **Every model change is validated on an untouched control group** (5% of leads, never contacted) and made only if
   better in at least 90% of bootstrap resamples.
5. **Next-best-action by uplift** (which step changes the outcome, after costs and discounts), with 15% random
   choices logged with their probability, so every policy can be evaluated without bias.
6. **Call slots and discount money have a price**, re-solved at each decision from the CRM's own decision log (a bid
   price, as in revenue management), so a call or a coupon goes to the lead it helps most, not the lead who came
   first, and a monthly discount budget lasts the month.
7. **Everything is counted in rupees of extra profit**: the pipeline shows what comes in anyway and what the team can
   add, lead by lead, and orders the work by it; a coupon given by hand is checked first (the coupon guard); and the
   owner's planner values the team's work, one more counsellor and more discount money from the same numbers.

How each works: [HOW_IT_WORKS.md](HOW_IT_WORKS.md).

## 3. The metrics: honest means measured on outcomes nobody's actions shaped

- **ROC AUC on identical test rows**, with DeLong's 95% interval and paired test, for lead scoring on real data.
- **Feedback bias**: the mean predicted minus actual rate on people a randomised experiment left alone.
- **Honest log-loss**: log-loss on those people. It is a proper scoring rule, so it rewards ranking *and* honest
  probabilities at once: one number for "best overall".
- **Calibration by lead age**: the weighted mean of |expected minus actual| over the age groups of the leads.
- **Share of hindsight value** (call slots, discount budget): the part of the value of the scarce resource a rule
  captures, between not using it (0%) and the best allocation with hindsight (100%), scored with the simulator's true
  effects.
- **Money estimates against the truth** (pipeline, planner): the predicted total over the true total, with the
  simulator's true probabilities; and the share of the most the team could add that an order of work captures.

## 4. The results

| # | Claim | Ours | Best baseline | How measured | Data |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Lead scoring, **same rows and same inputs** as each of four public solutions | AUC higher for all four: **+0.004 to +0.030**; better in **30 of 30** new splits for each, every 95% interval above zero | their own models (AUC 0.864 to 0.972) | DeLong on their own test rows; 30 new 70/30 splits, corrected t-interval | X Education, 9,240 real leads ([published_benchmark.md](../ml/results/published_benchmark.md)) |
| R2 | Lead scoring **for new leads** (no post-contact column) | **AUC 0.874** with 9 columns | 0.8605 (MSc thesis, NCI 2025); 0.864 (the best leak-free public solution) | 50 stratified 80/20 splits (above 0.8605 in 98%); +0.011 on that solution's own rows (DeLong p 0.0009) | same |
| R3 | The published accuracies above 90% need leakage | refitted without post-contact columns those solutions fall to AUC 0.599, 0.785 and 0.862; no leak-free model here exceeds AUC 0.886 or 81.4% accuracy | none | same rows, their own models | same |
| R4 | Retraining that does not fool itself | **feedback bias +0.33 points**, so **88% removed** (95% interval 72% to 104%); not distinguishable from a model with no loop at all | naive retrain +2.35 points (22% of the true rate) | 50 repeats, corrected resampled t-interval | Hillstrom real randomised email experiment, 42,613 customers ([learning_loop.md](../ml/results/learning_loop.md)) |
| R5 | **Best deployable retraining method** on one proper scoring rule | lowest honest log-loss in **49 of 50** repeats | naive retrain; retraining on the control group only (the clinical-ML holdout approach); inverse-propensity weighting | same | same |
| R6 | Choosing the model honestly | wrong switch in **2 of 50** | the usual check (fit on the CRM's own data) picks the inflated model in **50 of 50** | same | same |
| R7 | **Learned lead ageing** against hand-set decay | **lowest log-loss of all** (0.3587) and lowest calibration error by lead age (3.4 points); leads 7 days and older over-predicted by +23% instead of +40% | log-loss: no lead age 0.3758; HubSpot-style decay −25% and −50% after a month 0.3747 and 0.3810; Salesforce-style inactivity cap 0.3758 (changes nothing: the leads are active); naive retrain 0.3812. Every log-loss difference has its 95% interval above zero. Calibration 4.5 to 8.4 points (interval above zero against no lead age, the inactivity cap and naive; not against the two HubSpot-style rules) | 1,078 decision points where the CRM did nothing (control group and random picks), out of fold, cluster bootstrap over people | three simulated 180-day histories made by the CRM ([lead_age_check.md](../ml/results/lead_age_check.md)) |
| R8 | Who gets an email: uplift against likelihood | **+2.6 extra visits per 1,000** at a 10% email budget (95% interval +0.5 to +4.7) | targeting by predicted response (what score-based CRMs do) | inverse-propensity estimates on held-out customers, paired bootstrap | Hillstrom, 64,000 customers ([hillstrom_uplift.md](../ml/results/hillstrom_uplift.md)) |
| R9 | Next-best-action profit | **3.5 times** the profit of lead-score targeting, **90.5%** of the oracle; beats the best fixed policy in **20 of 20** random worlds (median 83% of the oracle; champion/challenger 87%) | lead-score targeting, the tier playbook, emailing everyone | known true effects | simulator ([nba_policy_comparison.md](../ml/results/nba_policy_comparison.md), [nba_robustness.md](../ml/results/nba_robustness.md)) |
| R10 | A/B statistics that can be trusted | 3.7% false alarms on A/A tests, 95.2% interval coverage, 79.8% power at the planned size; in 36 tests inside six histories: 15 correct, 15 real effects missed where the audience was too small, 6 still running, **0 wrong** | the targets: at most 5%, 95%, 80% | 4,000 simulated tests per check; six histories | ([ab_engine_check.md](../ml/results/ab_engine_check.md), [history_runs.md](../ml/results/history_runs.md)) |
| R11 | The CRM's total impact | worked-on leads bought within 30 days **+12.5 points** more often than the untouched control group (31.0% against 18.6%; 95% interval +8.6 to +15.8); positive in 6 of 6 histories | none | six simulated histories pooled | ([history_runs.md](../ml/results/history_runs.md)) |
| R12 | The live system continues its history exactly | every learner's daily chance to buy: largest difference **1.1e-16** over 145 learners, on a 60-day history with campaigns, an A/B test with coupons and visits after email clicks | none | `python -m app.cli simulation self-check` | simulated |
| R13 | The loop inside the product | predicts the untouched control group better than a naive retrain in **31 of 36** learning runs; over-states its buying by +23% in the final runs against +59% for the naive retrain; the usual check would pick the naive model in **35 of 36**; swaps models only 7 times in 36 runs. Against the model learning the steps' effects itself: better in 10 runs, worse in 7, the same in 19 (too few control-group decisions yet), mean log-loss 0.4108 against 0.4144 | naive retrain; the model learning the effects itself | 36 learning runs, judged on the control group | six simulated histories ([history_runs.md](../ml/results/history_runs.md)) |
| R14 | **Capacity-aware next-best-action** | with call-worthy decisions at 2 to 8 times the capacity, the re-solved slot price captures **95% to 97%** of the hindsight value (+₹23,258 to +₹88,039 a day at 20 calls a day); with demand doubling half-way through, 94.8% and 96.5%; with spare capacity the same as first come, first served | first come, first served 41% to 70%; a fixed daily price about 89% | 10 simulated runs of 60 days per scenario, the production pricing code, scored with the true effects, 95% intervals across runs | simulator ([capacity_check.md](../ml/results/capacity_check.md), figure `capacity_share.png`) |
| R15 | What-if paths predict what learners do next | Brier score **0.541** on average for the next three days' reaction; better than the stage-only mix in **4 of 6** histories | 0.545 per stage ignoring the step; 0.561 one mix for everyone | out of time in each history: learned before two thirds of it, tested on the later decisions (about 2,000 each), weighted by 1/probability | six simulated histories ([paths_check.md](../ml/results/paths_check.md)) |

Not significant with three histories | naive retrain +23.2 (+12.3 to +34.4); the paper's cut-off estimator +1.7 (−1.0 to +4.8) | 11 histories of 180 days in five settings, 10% evaluation group never contacted, paired cluster bootstrap | simulated histories ([anchored_check.md](../ml/results/anchored_check.md)) |

## 5. Where it does not win

- **Uplift learners on real data.** At a 10% budget our interpretable uplift model is significantly better than score
  targeting and the gradient-boosting learners, but level with the linear T-learner and class transformation (−0.2
  and +0.1 visits per 1,000, not significant); at larger budgets no policy is significantly better than targeting by
  response.
- **Ranking alone.** Naive retraining ranks as well as ours (honest AUC 0.637 against 0.638); the damage is to the
  probabilities, which is exactly what decides who is worth a call or a coupon.
- **When nothing works.** In a simulated world where no step changes anything, our model still contacts about half of
  the leads on estimation noise and loses ₹18,671 per 1,000 leads; the right answer (contact nobody) loses nothing. A
  confidence bound on the uplift would avoid this.
- **Hidden effects.** When most of a step's effect runs through things the interpretable model cannot see, the
  flexible model does better (it won 6 of 10 such worlds); the champion/challenger rule picked the better family in
  13 of 20 worlds.
- **Control groups are small** (5%). Our control-group check makes the right switch only when the difference is clear
  (11 of 50 on the real experiment) and the wrong one rarely (2 of 50). Inside the product, the loop still
  over-states the control group's buying (+23% in the final runs); most of the gap sits in leads older than a week
  ([followups_check.md](../ml/results/followups_check.md)), and later follow-ups inside the outcome window explain part
  of it (from +24.5% to +16.9% with one touch per 14 days).
- **A/B tests on small audiences** miss real effects (15 of 30 in the histories); the plan shown before sending warns
  when an audience is smaller than the planned size.
- **What-if paths are only a little better than a simpler guess**: better than the stage-only mix in 4 of 6
  histories (mean Brier 0.541 against 0.545).
- **The random learning steps cost money in simulation** (R18). With none, the CRM earned more in 12 of 14 simulated
  worlds (₹567 per lead on average), and 5% was not clearly better than 15%. The product keeps 15%: without random
  steps nothing can be measured (which step works, an honest check of a new policy), and the CRM could not notice
  when the world changes. The owner can change `exploration_rate`; this is a business choice, not a proven gain.
- **The step effects from the control group are not proven better** (R17). At the product's settings they are better
  on average and never the worst, but the 95% intervals include zero with three histories. Without random steps they
  are worse on average (+3.3, −3.3 to +10.1), and the research paper's cut-off estimator is clearly worse there (+25.2,
  +9.0 to +44.0): a lead the CRM leaves alone now is usually followed up at its next trigger, so the cut-off measures
  acting now against acting later, not against never.
- **The capacity and money results are simulated.** The true effects of a call or a coupon come from the simulator,
  and the next-best-action model was trained on a randomised campaign from the same simulator: the best case for the
  model (with perfect predictions, the discount budget would earn 22% to 32% more than with the model's, R19). The
  cart-recovery result rests on the simulator's assumption that coupons barely move people already at checkout. The
  prices need a week of decisions before they are used, and until then the CRM falls back to first come, first served.
- **The planner's estimates are rough.** One more counsellor is under-estimated by 11% when call demand only just
  exceeds the slots; 20% more discount money is over-estimated by up to 15% when the budget is tight (R22). The page
  says "about".
- **The coupon guard is a warning, not a rule.** For coupons to leads picked at random, 20% to 26% of the coupons it
  stops would have paid (R20), so it asks for a confirmation instead of refusing (except for the control group).
- **Simulated evidence** (R7, R9 to R15, R17 to R23) describes the documented simulator, not a market. The claims
  about real data rest on X Education (R1 to R3) and Hillstrom (R4 to R6, R8).
- **Simulated numbers move between versions.** Version 7.1 changed how the score's update treats the CRM's own steps
  (each step's effect from the control group), so its histories are different draws from version 7.0's (same seeds).
  Quote the current files.
- **The histories were made before the coupon rules.** The studies built on simulated histories (R7, R10 to R13,
  R15, R17) ran before 27 October 2026, when the CRM could still give a second coupon to someone who held an open one
  (in a fresh install's six-month history, 471 of 2,388 coupon decisions, 20%). Since then a person holds at most one
  open coupon and gets at most one coupon a week, so re-running those studies gives somewhat different simulated numbers; the real-data results (R1 to
  R6, R8) and the money studies (R19 to R22, their own simulator) are not affected.
- **Simulated histories follow the clock.** A history ends at the moment it is made, so re-running the studies built
  on histories (R7, R15 and the six-history parts of R10, R11 and R13) gives slightly different simulated numbers, for
  example 7,212 or 7,213 visits in the starting history of a fresh install depending on the hour. Exact repeats would
  need a fixed end time; the real-data results (R1 to R6, R8) and the fixed-calendar simulations (R9, R14 and the A/A
  checks of R10) already repeat exactly.
- Two papers in the comparison (Jadli et al. 2022, Yim et al. 2024) do not list their inputs; we compare with their
  reported numbers and say so.
- **Not one of the four re-run solutions:** the Kaggle notebook "Lead Scoring - A Logistic Regression Study" (the
  classic case-study notebook, by the dataset's uploader) was compared once, on 3 to 5 October 2026: on its own rows,
  its 12 columns and its cut-off rule our model scored AUC 0.903 against 0.88 and accuracy 82.25% against 80.48%
  (McNemar p = 0.004). That comparison's script was not kept, so it is not among the results that this repository
  reproduces, and the claim in R1 rests on the four solutions re-run above. That notebook's model also uses Last
  Activity, which is partly filled in after a lead is contacted.

## 6. To our knowledge

We found no lead-scoring or CRM paper that measures or removes the CRM's own effect from retraining (searched 2 and 8
October 2026; closest: clinical prediction models, Liley et al., AISTATS 2021; holdout sets for safe model updating,
Haidar-Wehbe et al. 2022; and performative prediction, Perdomo et al. 2020). For call capacity, the method is not new:
bid prices come from revenue management (Talluri and van Ryzin 1998) and re-solved dual prices from online linear
programming (Agrawal, Wang and Ye 2014). What we found in CRM and uplift work (searched 20 October 2026) allocates a
budget once over a whole customer list; we did not find next-best-action that prices a team's daily call capacity for
decisions arriving through the day. Claim both as "to our knowledge", never as "the first".

For the money features the methods are not new either: a dual price on a coupon budget for customers who arrive one
at a time is used in e-commerce (Dai et al. 2024 at Meituan, with a Lagrange multiplier adjusted during the day;
Zhang et al., BCORLE, NeurIPS 2021; Zhao et al., KDD 2019); uplift targeting beats response targeting when many
customers would buy anyway (Radcliffe and Surry 2011, "sure things"); marketing-mix models split sales into a
baseline and an incremental part for a whole market; and sales-force sizing has its own models (Lodish 1971; Zoltners,
Sinha and Lorimer 2004). What we did not find (searched 20 and 25 October 2026), in CRM products or papers: a pipeline
split lead by lead into what comes in anyway and what the team can add, from an honest score and an uplift model; a
check of a discount given by hand against the chance to buy without it; one decision that prices counsellor time and
discount money together, from the CRM's own decision log; and a planner that values one more counsellor or more
discount money by replaying the CRM's own priced decisions. Claim these as "to our knowledge" too.

## 7. Reproduce

From the project folder, with the backend's Python, after the first start (it trains the starting models):

```bash
python ml/run_experiments.py                     # E1 to E9; "quick" skips the slow ones (E2b, E6, E8, E8b)
python ml/run_experiments.py E7                  # one experiment
python ml/experiments/history_seeds.py           # the six 180-day histories behind R10, R11, R13 (about an hour)
python ml/experiments/anchored_histories.py --out WORK --seeds 2026 11 12 --settings c5_e15 c5_e05 c5_e00
python ml/experiments/anchored_histories.py --out WORK --seeds 2026 --settings c0_e15 c0_e00
python ml/experiments/anchored_check.py WORK/*   # R17 from those 11 histories (E8; c0_*: no control group)
python ml/experiments/exploration_check.py       # R18 (E8b, about 45 minutes)
python ml/experiments/money_check.py             # R19 to R22 (E9, under a minute)
python ml/experiments/followups_check.py         # where the loop's remaining gap comes from (about 20 minutes)
python -m app.cli simulation self-check          # R12 (run in backend/)
python scripts/latency_check.py                  # R16 (on a running system)
pip install -r ml/requirements.txt               # matplotlib, for the figures
```

Every study runs in its own temporary copy of the project, so your own database and models are never touched.

| Experiment | Script | Results |
|---|---|---|
| E1 lead scoring on real data | `model_benchmark.py` | `model_benchmark.md` |
| E1b against published solutions | `published_benchmark.py` | `published_benchmark.md` |
| E2 next-best-action on a real experiment | `hillstrom_uplift.py` | `hillstrom_uplift.md`, `figures/hillstrom_*.png` |
| E2b when the assumptions are wrong | `nba_robustness.py` | `nba_robustness.md` |
| E3 the learning loop on real data | `learning_loop.py` | `learning_loop.md` |
| E4 the A/B engine | `ab_engine_check.py` | `ab_engine_check.md` |
| E5 what-if paths | `paths_check.py` | `paths_check.md` |
| E6 learned lead ageing | `lead_age_check.py` | `lead_age_check.md` |
| E7 capacity-aware next-best-action | `capacity_check.py` | `capacity_check.md`, `figures/capacity_share.png` |
| E8 each step's effect from the CRM's own experiment, inside the product | `anchored_histories.py`, `anchored_check.py` | `anchored_check.md` |
| E8b what the random learning steps cost | `exploration_check.py` | `exploration_check.md` |
| E9 the money features: discount budget, coupon guard, pipeline in rupees, planner | `money_check.py` | `money_check.md`, `figures/money_budget_share.png` |
| Policy comparison (R9) | `python -m app.cli train uplift` | `nba_policy_comparison.md` |

import { QueryCache, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { ApiError, ThemeProvider } from "@xedu/shared/lib";
import { ToastProvider } from "@xedu/shared/ui";
import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { RouterProvider } from "react-router/dom";
import { router } from "./app/router";
import { SessionProvider } from "./app/SessionProvider";

const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  queryCache: new QueryCache(),
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 15_000,
      refetchOnWindowFocus: true,
      // a 4xx answer will not change by asking again
      retry: (count, error) => !(error instanceof ApiError && error.status >= 400 && error.status < 500) && count < 2,
    },
  },
});

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <ThemeProvider>
      <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
        <ToastProvider>
          <SessionProvider>
            <RouterProvider router={router} />
          </SessionProvider>
        </ToastProvider>
      </QueryClientProvider>
    </ThemeProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);

import { createHttpClient } from "@xedu/shared/lib";

const TOKEN_KEY = "xe-crm-token";

export function getToken(): string | null {
  try {
    return localStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY);
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

export function setToken(token: string | null): void {
  try {
    if (token) localStorage.setItem(TOKEN_KEY, token);
    else localStorage.removeItem(TOKEN_KEY);
  } catch {
    /* storage blocked: the session lasts until the tab closes */
  }
}

let onSignedOut: () => void = () => {};

/** The app registers what happens when the server says the session has ended. */
export function setSignedOutHandler(fn: () => void): void {
  onSignedOut = fn;
}

/** The CRM API: every path is relative to /api/v1/crm. */
export const api = createHttpClient({
  base: "/api/v1/crm",
  token: getToken,
  onUnauthorized: () => {
    setToken(null);
    onSignedOut();
  },
});

/** The public part of the API (the course catalogue), shared with the website. */
export const publicApi = createHttpClient({ base: "/api/v1" });

/** Queries used on more than one page (each page keeps its own queries next to it). */
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { useMemo } from "react";
import { api, publicApi } from "./client";
import type { Capacity, SimulationStatus, Stats } from "./types";

export function useStats(refetchInterval = 30_000, enabled = true) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ["stats"], queryFn: () => api.get<Stats>("/stats"), refetchInterval, enabled });
}

export function useCapacity(refetchInterval = 30_000) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ["capacity"], queryFn: () => api.get<Capacity>("/capacity"), refetchInterval });
}

export function useSimulation(refetchInterval = 20_000, enabled = true) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ["simulation"],
    queryFn: () => api.get<SimulationStatus>("/simulation"),
    refetchInterval,
    enabled,
  });
}

export interface CourseSummary {
  slug: string;
  title: string;
  domain: string;
  price: number;
}

/** The course catalogue (titles by slug); it changes only when the backend's catalogue file changes. */
export function useCourses() {
  const q = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["courses"],
    queryFn: () => publicApi.get<{ courses: CourseSummary[] }>("/courses"),
    staleTime: Infinity,
  });
  return useMemo(() => {
    const bySlug = new Map((q.data?.courses ?? []).map((c) => [c.slug, c]));
    return {
      list: q.data?.courses ?? [],
      title: (slug: string | null | undefined) => (slug ? (bySlug.get(slug)?.title ?? slug.replace(/-/g, " ")) : ""),
    };
  }, [q.data]);
}

// @vitest-environment jsdom
import { cleanup, render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";

function session(role: Me["role"], can: Me["can"]): SessionState {
  return {
    me: { id: 1, name: "Test", email: "t@example.com", role, can } as unknown as Me,
    checking: false,
    signIn: async () => {
      throw new Error("not used");
    },
    signOut: () => {},
    can: (area) => can.includes(area),
  };
}

function open(path: string, s: SessionState) {
  const router = createMemoryRouter(
    [
      {
        element: <RequireRole area="team" />,
        children: [{ path: "/team", element: <p>Team page with Add an account</p> }],
      },
    ],
    { initialEntries: [path] },
  );
  render(
    <SessionContext.Provider value={s}>
      <RouterProvider router={router} />
    </SessionContext.Provider>,
  );
}

describe("RequireRole", () => {
  it("shows an admin page to an admin", () => {
    open("/team", session("admin", ["team", "audit", "marketing", "leads"]));
    expect(screen.getByText("Team page with Add an account")).toBeTruthy();
  });

  it("tells a counsellor the page is not part of their role, and offers their start page", () => {
    open("/team", session("counsellor", ["leads"]));
    expect(screen.queryByText("Team page with Add an account")).toBeNull();
    expect(screen.getByText("This page is not part of your role")).toBeTruthy();
    expect(screen.getByRole("link", { name: "Back to your start page" }).getAttribute("href")).toBe("/actions");
  });
});

import { buttonClass, EmptyState, Spinner } from "@xedu/shared/ui";
import { Lock } from "lucide-react";
import { Link, Navigate, Outlet, useLocation } from "react-router";
import type { Me } from "../api/types";
import { useSession } from "./session";

/** The signed-in part of the CRM: a spinner while a saved session is checked, the sign-in page without one. */
export function RequireSession() {
  const { me, checking } = useSession();
  const location = useLocation();
  if (checking) {
    return (
      <div className="flex min-h-screen items-center justify-center">
        <Spinner label="Opening the CRM" />
      </div>
    );
  }
  if (!me) return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location.pathname + location.search }} />;
  if (me.must_change_password && location.pathname !== "/account") return <Navigate to="/account" replace />;
  return <Outlet />;
}

/** The start page: counsellors start with their tasks, everyone else with the overview. */
export function Home() {
  const { me } = useSession();
  return <Navigate to={me?.role === "counsellor" ? "/actions" : "/overview"} replace />;
}

const WHO: Record<Me["can"][number], string> = {
  team: "admins",
  audit: "admins",
  marketing: "admins and marketing",
  leads: "the team",
};

/** A page only some roles may use (opened from an old link or typed in): a plain message instead of a broken page.
 * The API refuses the data anyway; this keeps the screen honest. */
export function RequireRole({ area }: { area: Me["can"][number] }) {
  const { can, me } = useSession();
  if (can(area)) return <Outlet />;
  return (
    <div className="rounded-md border border-line bg-surface px-4">
      <EmptyState
        icon={Lock}
        title="This page is not part of your role"
        action={
          <Link to={me?.role === "counsellor" ? "/actions" : "/overview"} className={buttonClass("secondary", "sm")}>
            Back to your start page
          </Link>
        }
      >
        It is for {WHO[area]}. Ask an admin if you need something on it.
      </EmptyState>
    </div>
  );
}

import { createContext, useContext } from "react";
import type { Me, Member } from "../api/types";

export interface SessionState {
  me: Me | null;
  /** True while the first check of a saved session is running. */
  checking: boolean;
  signIn: (email: string, password: string) => Promise<Member>;
  signOut: () => void;
  can: (area: Me["can"][number]) => boolean;
}

export const SessionContext = createContext<SessionState | null>(null);

export function useSession(): SessionState {
  const ctx = useContext(SessionContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error("useSession must be used inside SessionProvider");
  return ctx;
}

/** The signed-in person (only inside the signed-in part of the app). */
export function useMe(): Me {
  const { me } = useSession();
  if (!me) throw new Error("Not signed in");
  return me;
}

==========================================================================================

import { useQuery, useQueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { useCallback, useEffect, useMemo, useState, type ReactNode } from "react";
import { api, getToken, setSignedOutHandler, setToken } from "../api/client";
import type { Me, Member } from "../api/types";
import { SessionContext, type SessionState } from "./session";

/** Keeps the signed-in team member: the token in this browser, and who it belongs to (GET /me). */
export function SessionProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  const [hasToken, setHasToken] = useState(() => Boolean(getToken()));

  const me = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["me"],
    queryFn: () => api.get<Me>("/me"),
    enabled: hasToken,
    staleTime: 60_000,
  });

  const signOut = useCallback(() => {
    setToken(null);
    setHasToken(false);
    qc.clear();
  }, [qc]);

  useEffect(() => setSignedOutHandler(signOut), [signOut]);

  const signIn = useCallback(
    async (email: string, password: string) => {
      const r = await api.post<{ token: string; member: Member }>("/auth/login", { email, password });
      setToken(r.token);
      setHasToken(true);
      await qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["me"] });
      return r.member;
    },
    [qc],
  );

  const value = useMemo<SessionState>(() => {
    const m = hasToken ? (me.data ?? null) : null;
    return {
      me: m,
      checking: hasToken && me.isPending,
      signIn,
      signOut,
      can: (area) => Boolean(m?.can.includes(area)),
    };
  }, [hasToken, me.data, me.isPending, signIn, signOut]);

  return <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</SessionContext.Provider>;
}

import { Badge } from "@xedu/shared/ui";
import type { AbVerdict } from "../api/types";

/** The test's state in two or three words; the full verdict is in the tooltip and on the test's page. */
export function VerdictBadge({ v, state }: { v: AbVerdict | null; state: string }) {
  if (state === "draft") return <Badge>Draft</Badge>;
  if (!v) return <Badge tone="info">Running</Badge>;
  const tone =
    v.status === "winner"
      ? "good"
      : v.status === "broken" || v.status === "loser"
        ? "bad"
        : v.status === "running"
          ? "info"
          : "neutral";
  const label =
    v.status === "winner"
      ? `Variant ${v.winner ?? ""} wins`
      : v.status === "loser"
        ? "A variant did worse"
        : v.status === "broken"
          ? "Split looks broken"
          : v.status === "running"
            ? "Running"
            : v.status === "waiting"
              ? "Not sent"
              : "No clear difference";
  return (
    <Badge tone={tone} title={v.headline}>
      {label}
    </Badge>
  );
}

import { cn, int, money, plural } from "@xedu/shared/lib";
import { Badge } from "@xedu/shared/ui";
import type { Capacity } from "../api/types";

/** One cell per call slot while the day's capacity is small enough to count; a plain bar above that. */
function SlotCells({ used, capacity }: { used: number; capacity: number }) {
  const shown = Math.min(used, capacity);
  if (capacity <= 40) {
    return (
      <div aria-hidden className="flex gap-[3px]">
        {Array.from({ length: capacity }, (_, i) => (
          <span
            key={i}
            className={cn("h-3 flex-1 rounded-[2px]", i < shown ? "bg-brand" : "bg-sunken ring-1 ring-inset ring-line")}
          />
        ))}
      </div>
    );
  }
  return (
    <div aria-hidden className="h-3 overflow-hidden rounded-[2px] bg-sunken ring-1 ring-inset ring-line">
      <div className="h-full bg-brand" style={{ width: `${(100 * shown) / Math.max(capacity, 1)}%` }} />
    </div>
  );
}

function priceSentence(c: Capacity): string {
  if (c.full) return "Today's call slots are used up. New decisions choose the best step without a call.";
  if (c.policy === "fcfs") return "Calls are given out first come, first served until the slots are used.";
  if (!c.price) return "Calls are not scarce right now, so every call worth making gets a slot.";
  return `A call is created only when it adds more than ${money(c.price)} over the best step without a call.`;
}

function teamSentence(c: Capacity): string {
  if (c.full) return "Today's call slots are used up. New decisions choose the best step without a call.";
  if (c.policy === "fcfs") return "Calls are given out first come, first served until the slots are used.";
  if (!c.price) return "Calls are not scarce right now, so every call worth making gets a slot.";
  return "Calls are scarce, so the CRM keeps them for the learners a call helps most; the others get the best step without a call.";
}

/**
 * Today's call slots (capacity-aware next-best-action): how many are used, and the price a call has to beat. The
 * price is the extra profit of the call that would otherwise be crowded out later today.
 */
export function CapacityMeter({
  capacity: c,
  className,
  showPrice = false,
}: {
  capacity: Capacity;
  className?: string;
  /** The rupee price of a slot: for the Next-best-action page, not for the team's own call list. */
  showPrice?: boolean;
}) {
  const label = `${int(c.calls_today)} of ${int(c.capacity)} call slots used today`;
  return (
    <div className={cn("rounded-md border border-line bg-surface px-4 py-3.5", className)}>
      <div className="flex flex-wrap items-baseline gap-x-3 gap-y-1">
        <h2 className="text-[14px] font-semibold text-ink">Call slots today</h2>
        <Badge tone={c.policy === "priced" ? "brand" : "neutral"} variant="outline">
          {c.policy === "priced" ? "Priced slots" : "First come, first served"}
        </Badge>
        <span className="ml-auto text-[13px] text-muted">
          <span className="num font-semibold text-ink">{int(c.calls_today)}</span> of{" "}
          <span className="num">{int(c.capacity)}</span> used
        </span>
      </div>
      <div
        role="meter"
        aria-label={label}
        aria-valuemin={0}
        aria-valuemax={c.capacity}
        aria-valuenow={c.calls_today}
        className="mt-2.5"
      >
        <SlotCells used={c.calls_today} capacity={c.capacity} />
      </div>
      {showPrice ? (
        <div className="mt-3 flex flex-wrap items-baseline gap-x-6 gap-y-1.5">
          <p className="text-[13.5px] text-ink">
            Price of a call slot{" "}
            <span className="num text-[16px] font-semibold">
              {c.full ? "Full" : c.price === null ? "Not set" : money(c.price)}
            </span>
          </p>
          <p className="min-w-0 flex-1 basis-80 text-[13px] text-muted">{priceSentence(c)}</p>
        </div>
      ) : (
        <p className="mt-3 text-[13px] text-muted">{teamSentence(c)}</p>
      )}
      <p className="mt-2 text-[12.5px] text-muted">
        Worked out from {plural(c.candidates, "decision")} that could have used a call in the last{" "}
        {plural(c.days_seen || c.lookback_days, "day")}: about {Math.round(c.per_day)} a day.
        {c.note ? ` ${c.note}` : ""}
      </p>
    </div>
  );
}

import { cn, useChartColors } from "@xedu/shared/lib";
import { Segmented } from "@xedu/shared/ui";
import { useId, useState, type ReactNode } from "react";
import {
  Bar,
  BarChart,
  CartesianGrid,
  Line,
  LineChart,
  ResponsiveContainer,
  Tooltip,
  XAxis,
  YAxis,
  type TooltipContentProps,
} from "recharts";

export interface Series<K extends string = string> {
  key: K;
  label: string;
  /** A dashed line (for an estimate next to what happened), so lines differ by more than their colour. */
  dashed?: boolean;
}

interface ChartProps<T extends object> {
  title: string;
  description?: ReactNode;
  data: readonly T[];
  /** The key of the x value of each row (a date or a category). */
  x: keyof T & string;
  series: Series<keyof T & string>[];
  kind?: "line" | "bar";
  height?: number;
  /** Formats values (axis, tooltip and table). */
  format: (v: number) => string;
  /** A shorter format for the y axis (defaults to format). */
  axisFormat?: (v: number) => string;
  xFormat?: (v: string) => string;
  className?: string;
  footer?: ReactNode;
  /** A marker on every point of a line (when each point is an event, such as a learning run). */
  dots?: boolean;
  /** Shown instead of an empty chart when every value is zero or missing (a new business has no data yet). */
  empty?: string;
}

function Legend({ series, colors, kind }: { series: Series[]; colors: readonly string[]; kind: "line" | "bar" }) {
  if (series.length < 2) return null;
  return (
    <ul className="flex flex-wrap gap-x-4 gap-y-1 px-4 pt-2 text-[12.5px] text-ink-2">
      {series.map((s, i) => (
        <li key={s.key} className="flex items-center gap-1.5">
          {kind === "line" && s.dashed ? (
            <svg aria-hidden width="16" height="4" viewBox="0 0 16 4">
              <line
                x1="0"
                y1="2"
                x2="16"
                y2="2"
                stroke={colors[i % colors.length]}
                strokeWidth="2"
                strokeDasharray="5 3"
              />
            </svg>
          ) : (
            <span
              aria-hidden
              className={kind === "line" ? "h-0.5 w-3.5 rounded-full" : "size-2.5 rounded-[2px]"}
              style={{ background: colors[i % colors.length] }}
            />
          )}
          {s.label}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

function TooltipBox({
  active,
  payload,
  label,
  format,
  xFormat,
}: Partial<TooltipContentProps<number, string>> & { format: (v: number) => string; xFormat?: (v: string) => string }) {
  if (!active || !payload?.length) return null;
  return (
    <div className="min-w-40 rounded-sm border border-line bg-raised px-3 py-2 text-[12.5px] shadow-overlay">
      <p className="mb-1 font-medium text-ink">{xFormat ? xFormat(String(label)) : String(label)}</p>
      {payload.map((p) => (
        <p key={String(p.dataKey)} className="flex items-center gap-2 text-ink-2">
          <span aria-hidden className="size-2 rounded-full" style={{ background: p.color }} />
          {p.name}
          <span className="num ml-auto pl-4 font-medium text-ink">
            {typeof p.value === "number" ? format(p.value) : "None"}
          </span>
        </p>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

function cell<T extends object>(row: T, key: keyof T & string): unknown {
  return (row as Record<string, unknown>)[key];
}

function DataTable<T extends object>({
  data,
  x,
  series,
  format,
  xFormat,
  title,
}: Pick<ChartProps<T>, "data" | "x" | "series" | "format" | "xFormat" | "title">) {
  return (
    <div className="max-h-72 overflow-auto">
      <table className="w-full border-collapse text-[13px]" aria-label={title}>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th
              scope="col"
              className="sticky top-0 border-b border-line bg-surface py-1.5 pr-3 text-left font-medium text-muted"
            >
              {x === "date" ? "Date" : ""}
            </th>
            {series.map((s) => (
              <th
                key={s.key}
                scope="col"
                className="sticky top-0 border-b border-line bg-surface py-1.5 pl-3 text-right font-medium text-muted"
              >
                {s.label}
              </th>
            ))}
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {data.map((r, i) => (
            <tr key={i}>
              <th scope="row" className="border-b border-line py-1.5 pr-3 text-left font-normal text-ink-2">
                {xFormat ? xFormat(String(cell(r, x))) : String(cell(r, x))}
              </th>
              {series.map((s) => {
                const v = cell(r, s.key);
                return (
                  <td key={s.key} className="num border-b border-line py-1.5 pl-3 text-right text-ink">
                    {typeof v === "number" ? format(v) : "None"}
                  </td>
                );
              })}
            </tr>
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  );
}

/**
 * A line or bar chart on one y axis, with a hover tooltip, a legend for two or more series, and a table view of the
 * same numbers (for screen readers, print, and anyone who prefers the figures).
 */
export function TrendChart<T extends object>({
  title,
  description,
  data,
  x,
  series,
  kind = "line",
  height = 220,
  format,
  axisFormat,
  xFormat,
  className,
  footer,
  dots = false,
  empty,
}: ChartProps<T>) {
  const c = useChartColors();
  const [view, setView] = useState<"chart" | "table">("chart");
  const titleId = useId();
  const tick = { fill: c.text, fontSize: 12 };
  const axis = axisFormat ?? format;
  // whole-number ticks only for counts: shares (0 to 1) and money need decimals between the integers
  const counts = data.every((r) =>
    series.every((s) => {
      const v = cell(r, s.key);
      return typeof v !== "number" || Number.isInteger(v);
    }),
  );
  const nothing =
    Boolean(empty) &&
    data.every((r) =>
      series.every((s) => {
        const v = cell(r, s.key);
        return v === null || v === undefined || v === 0;
      }),
    );
  const common = (
    <>
      <CartesianGrid vertical={false} stroke={c.grid} />
      <XAxis
        dataKey={x as string}
        tick={tick}
        tickLine={false}
        axisLine={{ stroke: c.axis }}
        tickFormatter={xFormat ? (v: string) => xFormat(String(v)) : undefined}
        minTickGap={18}
        interval="preserveStartEnd"
      />
      <YAxis
        tick={tick}
        tickLine={false}
        axisLine={false}
        width={56}
        tickFormatter={(v: number) => axis(v)}
        allowDecimals={!counts}
      />
      <Tooltip
        cursor={kind === "line" ? { stroke: c.axis, strokeWidth: 1 } : { fill: c.grid, opacity: 0.6 }}
        content={(p) => (
          <TooltipBox {...(p as Partial<TooltipContentProps<number, string>>)} format={format} xFormat={xFormat} />
        )}
      />
    </>
  );
  return (
    <figure aria-labelledby={titleId} className={cn("rounded-md border border-line bg-surface", className)}>
      <figcaption className="flex flex-wrap items-start gap-3 px-4 pt-3">
        <div className="min-w-0 flex-1">
          <p id={titleId} className="text-[14px] font-semibold text-ink">
            {title}
          </p>
          {description && <p className="mt-0.5 text-[12.5px] text-muted">{description}</p>}
        </div>
        <Segmented
          size="sm"
          label={`${title}: show as`}
          value={view}
          onChange={setView}
          options={[
            { value: "chart", label: "Chart" },
            { value: "table", label: "Table" },
          ]}
        />
      </figcaption>
      {view === "chart" && nothing ? (
        <p className="px-4 pb-4 pt-3 text-[13.5px] text-muted" style={{ minHeight: height / 2 }}>
          {empty}
        </p>
      ) : view === "chart" ? (
        <>
          <Legend series={series} colors={c.series} kind={kind} />
          <div className="px-2 pb-3 pt-2" style={{ height }}>
            <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
              {kind === "line" ? (
                <LineChart data={data as T[]} margin={{ top: 8, right: 12, bottom: 0, left: 0 }}>
                  {common}
                  {series.map((s, i) => (
                    <Line
                      key={s.key}
                      type="monotone"
                      dataKey={s.key as string}
                      name={s.label}
                      stroke={c.series[i % c.series.length]}
                      strokeWidth={2}
                      strokeDasharray={s.dashed ? "5 4" : undefined}
                      dot={
                        dots
                          ? {
                              r: 4,
                              fill: c.series[i % c.series.length],
                              stroke: c.surface,
                              strokeWidth: 2,
                              strokeDasharray: "none",
                            }
                          : false
                      }
                      activeDot={{ r: 5, stroke: c.surface, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "none" }}
                      isAnimationActive={false}
                      connectNulls
                    />
                  ))}
                </LineChart>
              ) : (
                <BarChart
                  data={data as T[]}
                  margin={{ top: 8, right: 12, bottom: 0, left: 0 }}
                  barGap={2}
                  barCategoryGap="24%"
                >
                  {common}
                  {series.map((s, i) => (
                    <Bar
                      key={s.key}
                      dataKey={s.key as string}
                      name={s.label}
                      fill={c.series[i % c.series.length]}
                      maxBarSize={24}
                      radius={[4, 4, 0, 0]}
                      isAnimationActive={false}
                    />
                  ))}
                </BarChart>
              )}
            </ResponsiveContainer>
          </div>
        </>
      ) : (
        <div className="px-4 pb-3 pt-2">
          <DataTable data={data} x={x} series={series} format={format} xFormat={xFormat} title={title} />
        </div>
      )}
      {footer && <div className="border-t border-line px-4 py-2.5 text-[12.5px] text-muted">{footer}</div>}
    </figure>
  );
}

export interface IntervalRow {
  label: ReactNode;
  value: number | null;
  low?: number | null;
  high?: number | null;
  note?: ReactNode;
  emphasis?: boolean;
}

/** Two ends of an interval, naming a shared unit once: "+10.3 points", "+24.8 points" -> "+10.3 to +24.8 points". */
function range(low: string, high: string): string {
  const unit = / [a-z]+$/i.exec(low)?.[0];
  return unit && high.endsWith(unit) ? `${low.slice(0, -unit.length)} to ${high}` : `${low} to ${high}`;
}

/**
 * Estimates with their 95% interval on one shared scale (a dot and a whisker per row), for policy values and A/B
 * test lifts. A zero line is drawn when the scale crosses zero.
 */
export function IntervalPlot({
  rows,
  format,
  label,
  className,
}: {
  rows: IntervalRow[];
  format: (v: number) => string;
  label: string;
  className?: string;
}) {
  const c = useChartColors();
  const values = rows.flatMap((r) => [r.value, r.low, r.high]).filter((v): v is number => typeof v === "number");
  if (!values.length) return null;
  let lo = Math.min(0, ...values);
  let hi = Math.max(0, ...values);
  const pad = (hi - lo || 1) * 0.06;
  lo -= pad;
  hi += pad;
  const at = (v: number) => `${((v - lo) / (hi - lo)) * 100}%`;
  const zero = lo < 0 && hi > 0;
  return (
    <div role="table" aria-label={label} className={cn("text-[13.5px]", className)}>
      {rows.map((r, i) => (
        <div
          key={i}
          role="row"
          className="grid grid-cols-[minmax(0,13rem)_minmax(0,1fr)_8.5rem] items-center gap-x-4 border-b border-line py-2.5 last:border-b-0"
        >
          <div role="cell" className="min-w-0">
            <p className={cn("truncate", r.emphasis ? "font-medium text-ink" : "text-ink-2")}>{r.label}</p>
            {r.note && <p className="truncate text-[12px] text-muted">{r.note}</p>}
          </div>
          <div role="cell" aria-hidden className="relative h-5">
            <span className="absolute inset-x-0 top-1/2 h-px -translate-y-1/2" style={{ background: c.grid }} />
            {zero && <span className="absolute inset-y-0 w-px" style={{ left: at(0), background: c.axis }} />}
            {typeof r.low === "number" && typeof r.high === "number" && (
              <span
                className="absolute top-1/2 h-0.5 -translate-y-1/2 rounded-full"
                style={{ left: at(r.low), width: `calc(${at(r.high)} - ${at(r.low)})`, background: c.series[0] }}
              />
            )}
            {typeof r.value === "number" && (
              <span
                className="absolute top-1/2 size-2.5 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2 rounded-full"
                style={{ left: at(r.value), background: c.series[0], boxShadow: `0 0 0 2px ${c.surface}` }}
              />
            )}
          </div>
          <div role="cell" className="text-right">
            <p className="num font-medium text-ink">
              {typeof r.value === "number" ? format(r.value) : "Not enough data"}
            </p>
            {typeof r.low === "number" && typeof r.high === "number" && (
              <p className="num text-[12px] text-muted">{range(format(r.low), format(r.high))}</p>
            )}
          </div>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
